{{Short description|Nonlocal mathematical operator}}
In [[mathematical analysis]], the '''fractional Laplacian''' is an operator that generalizes the notion of the [[Laplace operator]] to fractional powers of spatial derivatives. It is frequently used in the analysis of [[Nonlocal operator|nonlocal]] partial differential equations, especially in geometry and diffusion theory.

== Definition ==

In the literature, the definition of the fractional Laplacian often varies, but most of the time those definitions are equivalent. The following is a short overview proven by Kwaśnicki, M.<ref name=":0">{{cite journal |last1=Kwaśnicki |first1=Mateusz |year=2017 |title=Ten equivalent definitions of the fractional Laplace operator |journal=Fractional Calculus and Applied Analysis |volume=20 |pages=7–51 |arxiv=1507.07356 |doi=10.1515/fca-2017-0002}}</ref>

Let <math>p \in [1, \infty)</math> and <math>\mathcal{X} := L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)</math> or let <math>\mathcal{X} := C_0(\mathbb{R}^n)</math> or <math>\mathcal{X} := C_{bu}(\mathbb{R}^n)</math>, where:
* <math>C_0(\mathbb{R}^n)</math> denotes the space of continuous functions <math>f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}</math> that [[vanish at infinity]], i.e., <math>\forall \varepsilon > 0, \exists K \subset \mathbb{R}^n</math> compact such that <math>|f(x)| < \epsilon</math> for all <math>x \notin K</math>.
* <math>C_{bu}(\mathbb{R}^n)</math> denotes the space of bounded uniformly continuous functions <math>f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}</math>, i.e., functions that are uniformly continuous, meaning <math>\forall \epsilon > 0, \exists \delta > 0</math> such that <math>|f(x) - f(y)| < \epsilon</math> for all <math>x, y \in \mathbb{R}^n</math> with <math>|x - y| < \delta</math>, and bounded, meaning <math>\exists M > 0</math> such that <math>|f(x)| \leq M</math> for all <math>x \in \mathbb{R}^n</math>.

Additionally, let <math>s \in (0, 1)</math>.

=== Fourier definition ===
If we further restrict to <math>p \in [1,2]</math>, we get

:<math>(-\Delta)^s f := \mathcal{F}_{ \xi}^{-1}(| \xi|^{2s} \mathcal{F}(f))</math>

This definition uses the [[Fourier transform]] for <math>f \in L^p( \mathbb{R}^n)</math>. This definition can also be broadened through the [[Bessel potential]] to all <math>p \in [1, \infty)</math>.

=== Singular operator ===
The Laplacian can also be viewed as a [[singular integral operator]] which is defined as the following limit taken in <math>\mathcal{X}</math>.

:<math> (-\Delta)^s f(x) = \frac{4^s \Gamma(\frac{d}{2}+s)}{\pi^{d/2} |\Gamma(-s)|} \lim_{r \to 0^+} \int\limits_{\mathbb{R}^d \setminus B_r (x)}{\frac{f(x)-f(y)}{|x-y|^{d+2s}}\,dy} </math>

=== Generator of C<sub>0</sub>-semigroup ===
Using the fractional heat-[[C0-semigroup|semigroup]] which is the family of operators <math>\{P_t \}_{t \in [0,\infty)}</math>, we can define the fractional Laplacian through its generator.

:<math> -(-\Delta)^s f(x) = \lim_{t \to 0^+} \frac{P_t f - f}{ t}.  </math>

It is to note that the generator is not the fractional Laplacian <math>(-\Delta)^s</math> but the negative of it <math>-(-\Delta)^s</math>. The operator <math>P_t : \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{X}</math> is defined by

:<math> P_t f := p_t * f </math>,

where <math>*</math> is the [[convolution]] of two functions and <math>p_t := \mathcal{F}^{-1}_{ \xi}(e^{ - t | \xi|^{2s}})</math>.

=== Distributional definition ===
For all [[Schwartz function]]s <math>\varphi</math>, the fractional Laplacian can be defined in a [[Distribution (mathematical analysis)|distributional]] sense by

:<math> \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} (-\Delta)^s f(y) \varphi(y) \, dy = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} f(x) (-\Delta)^s \varphi(x) \, dx </math>

where <math>(-\Delta)^s \varphi</math> is defined as in the Fourier definition.

=== Bochner's definition ===
The fractional Laplacian can be expressed using Bochner's integral as

:<math>
(-\Delta)^s f = \frac{1}{\Gamma(-\frac{s}{2})} \int_0^\infty \left( e^{t \Delta} f - f \right) t^{-1 - s/2} \, dt
</math>

where the integral is understood in the [[Bochner integral|Bochner sense]] for <math>\mathcal{X}</math>-valued functions.

=== Balakrishnan's definition ===
Alternatively, it can be defined via Balakrishnan's formula:

:<math>
(-\Delta)^s f = \frac{\sin \left( \frac{s \pi}{2} \right)}{\pi} \int_0^\infty (-\Delta) \left( s I - \Delta \right)^{-1} f \, s^{s/2 - 1} \, ds
</math>

with the integral interpreted as a Bochner integral for <math>\mathcal{X}</math>-valued functions.

=== Dynkin's definition ===
Another approach by Dynkin defines the fractional Laplacian as

:<math>
(-\Delta)^s f = \lim_{r \to 0^+} \frac{2^s \Gamma\left( \frac{d + s}{2} \right)}{\pi^{d/2} \Gamma\left( -\frac{s}{2} \right)} \int_{\mathbb{R}^d \setminus \overline{B}(x, r)} \frac{f(x + z) - f(x)}{|z|^d \left( |z|^2 - r^2 \right)^{s/2}} \, dz
</math>

with the limit taken in <math>\mathcal{X}</math>.

=== Quadratic form definition ===
In <math>\mathcal{X} = L^2</math>, the fractional Laplacian can be characterized via a [[quadratic form]]:

:<math>\langle (-\Delta)^{\frac{s}{2}} f, \varphi \rangle = \mathcal{E}(f, \varphi)</math>

where

:<math>
\mathcal{E}(f, g) = \frac{2^s \Gamma\left( \frac{d + s}{2} \right)}{2 \pi^{d/2} \Gamma\left( -\frac{s}{2} \right)} \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \frac{(f(y) - f(x)) (\overline{g(y)} - \overline{g(x)})}{|x - y|^{d + s}} \, dx \, dy
</math>

=== Inverse of the Riesz potential definition ===
When <math>s < d</math> and <math>\mathcal{X} = L^p</math> for <math>p \in [1, \frac{d}{s})</math>, the fractional Laplacian satisfies

:<math>
\frac{\Gamma\left( \frac{d - s}{2} \right)}{2^s \pi^{d/2} \Gamma\left( \frac{s}{2} \right)} \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \frac{(-\Delta)^s f(x + z)}{|z|^{d - s}} \, dz = f(x)
</math>

=== Harmonic extension definition ===
The fractional Laplacian can also be defined through harmonic extensions. Specifically, there exists a function <math>u(x, y)</math> such that

:<math>
\begin{cases}
\Delta_x u(x, y) + \alpha^2 c_\alpha^{2 / \alpha} y^{2 - 2/\alpha} \partial_y^2 u(x, y) = 0 & \text{for } y > 0, \\
u(x, 0) = f(x), \\
\partial_y u(x, 0) = -(-\Delta)^s f(x),
\end{cases}
</math>

where <math>c_\alpha = 2^{-\alpha} \frac{|\Gamma\left( -\frac{\alpha}{2} \right)|}{\Gamma\left( \frac{\alpha}{2} \right)}</math> and <math>u(\cdot, y)</math> is a function in <math>\mathcal{X}</math> that depends continuously on <math>y \in [0, \infty)</math> with <math>\|u(\cdot, y)\|_{\mathcal{X}}</math> bounded for all <math>y \geq 0</math>.

== Relation to other operators ==

=== Riesz transforms and the half-Laplacian ===

In dimension one, the [[Hilbert transform]] <math>\mathcal{H}</math> satisfies the identity
:<math>(-\Delta)^{1/2} = \mathcal{H} \circ \partial_x.</math>
This expresses the half-Laplacian as the composition of the Hilbert transform with the spatial derivative.

In higher dimensions <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math>, this generalizes naturally to the vector-valued [[Riesz transform]]. For a function <math>f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}</math>, the <math>j</math>-th Riesz transform is defined as the singular integral operator
:<math>R_j f(x) = c_n \, \mathrm{p.v.} \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \frac{x_j - y_j}{|x - y|^{n+1}} f(y)\, dy.</math>

Equivalently, it is a [[Multiplier (Fourier analysis)|Fourier multiplier]] with symbol
:<math>\widehat{R_j f}(\xi) = -i \frac{\xi_j}{|\xi|} \hat{f}(\xi).</math>

Letting <math>Rf = (R_1 f, \dots, R_n f)</math> and <math>\nabla f = (\partial_1 f, \dots, \partial_n f)</math>, we obtain the key identity:
:<math>(-\Delta)^{1/2} f = \sum_{j=1}^n R_j(\partial_j f) = \operatorname{div}(R f).</math>

This follows directly from the Fourier symbols:
:<math>\widehat{(-\Delta)^{1/2}f}(\xi) = |\xi| \hat{f}(\xi),\quad \widehat{R_j(\partial_j f)}(\xi) = \frac{\xi_j^2}{|\xi|} \hat{f}(\xi).</math>

Summing over <math>j</math> recovers <math>|\xi| \hat{f}(\xi)</math>, hence the identity holds in the sense of tempered distributions.
